summary: Informal podcast-style customer interview with Aurora Analytics about how they use Redwood Inference for productionizing ML features — focused on cost/latency tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, and the business impact. Capture of anecdotes for marketing/case study; agreed next steps for quotes, release waiver, and a short technical blurb for the engineering blog.
topics: Deployment mode: Dedicated vs Hosted decision
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, welcome — this is Jordan from Redwood. Thanks so much for joining the podcast-style interview today. We've got Lena, Marcus, and Sofia from Aurora Analytics. How's everyone doing?
00:08 Lena Patel: Hi Jordan, good morning, thanks for having us. Excited to share the story.
00:12 Marcus Lee: Morning — yeah, thanks.
00:15 Sofia Ruiz: Morning all.
00:18 Jordan Kim: Awesome. I'll kick off with a very quick intro of Redwood then we'll jump into Aurora's journey. Maya, feel free to chime in with technical bits.
00:28 Maya Ortiz: Yep, will do.
00:30 Jordan Kim: So Lena, can you give us the 30-second overview of Aurora — what you do and what prompted you to look for a different inference solution?
00:40 Lena Patel: Sure. Uh, Aurora Analytics is a B2B analytics platform that does natural language summaries and insight generation over customer time-series and log data. We ship a set of features inside our product — like auto-summaries, alert reasoning — and as that usage scaled, the cost and latency on our previous setup just started to balloon. We had an internal self-hosted model that, uh, worked fine for prototypes but once we hit real traffic it was expensive and fragile.
01:05 Jordan Kim: And what were the main pain points — was it mainly cost, or did latency and reliability factor in?
01:12 Lena Patel: All three. Cost for sure — token costs and GPU utilization. Latency was a user experience blocker when customers wanted interactive summaries. And reliability — we had spikes and queuing causing timeouts. We needed something predictable.
01:26 Marcus Lee: To add, the operational overhead. We were spending a lot of SRE cycles babysitting nodes and tuning batch sizes. We needed a partner that could give reliable SLAs and also let us control costs.
01:38 Jordan Kim: Cool. Maya, can you quickly describe what Aurora implemented on Redwood — was it Hosted API first or did they go Dedicated?
01:46 Maya Ortiz: They started Hosted during the POC for speed, then moved to Dedicated Reserved capacity about three months after the pilot. We helped them with model selection, quantization profiles, and batching settings. Also enabled prefix caching for common prompts which cut token usage.
01:59 Lena Patel: The migration was smoother than expected. The Redwood Console dashboards were actually super helpful to show cost per route and token breakdowns so we could optimize.
02:12 Jordan Kim: Nice, that's good to hear. Marcus, do you recall the key metrics that convinced leadership to commit to Dedicated?
02:20 Marcus Lee: Yeah, the three numbers: 40% cost reduction per effective request, median latency down from ~900ms to ~220ms for our common summaries, and an SLO uptime improvement, from low 99s to 99.9 after we set up the reserved capacity and fallback policies. That combination sold it.
02:39 Jordan Kim: That's a big jump. Any funny story or hiccup during cutover?
02:44 Lena Patel: Uh, we had one day where our prefix cache was mis-configured and we were double-sending context so billing looked inflated in the console. Maya helped spot it; turned out to be a client side join bug.
02:57 Maya Ortiz: Yep, caught it in tracing — the console trace made the root cause obvious.
03:03 Jordan Kim: For the marketing piece, listeners love numbers and anecdotes — so that's gold. Switching gears — technical deep dive slight — what models are you running and any custom tuning? Maya?
03:16 Maya Ortiz: They run a mix of open LLMs — a fine-tuned 7B variant for short summaries and a 13B quantized model for deep analysis. We recommended a 4-bit quantization for the 13B which saved memory with minimal quality regression. Also enabled continuous batching with a latency-first policy for interactive endpoints.
03:38 Marcus Lee: The 4-bit thing sounded scary at first but profile tests showed the quality delta was negligible for our use case.
03:45 Marcus Lee: One more note — we use model pinning so certain enterprise customers always get the 13B variant and not the cheaper 7B, that helped with billing fairness.
03:55 Jordan Kim: Love that. For the case study — what business outcome can we highlight? Marcus?
04:01 Marcus Lee: We increased user engagement on the insights tab by about 18% post-launch, and average session time went up. That was directly correlated to faster summaries and reduced failure rate. Also our churn signal for accounts using the feature decreased.
04:16 Lena Patel: The finance team also liked the predictable monthly committed cost versus the prior variable GPU consumption.
04:24 Jordan Kim: Perfect. Sofia, from a marketing perspective, what are you hoping to include in the case study and podcast?
04:31 Sofia Ruiz: Short customer quote, high-level numbers (cost down 40%, latency improved), a short blurb about technical partnership, and maybe a before/after screenshot or metric graphic. We'll want to edit the recording and get a sign-off on quotes.
04:43 Jordan Kim: Great. We'll send an outline and a release waiver.
04:46 Sofia Ruiz: Awesome.
04:48 Jordan Kim: I want to also surface a slightly technical question — security/compliance: Aurora handles PII. How did you approach data residency and key management? Lena?
04:59 Lena Patel: We have a mix — some workloads are in our VPC private deployment for regulated customers, other non-sensitive processing routes go via Redwood Hosted for speed. Redwood's KMS integration and audit logs gave the security team confidence.
05:15 Jordan Kim: Did you need SOC 2 docs or encryption attestation?
05:19 Lena Patel: Yes, SOC 2 and the KMS/HSM screenshots — Maya shared those during procurement which helped unblock compliance.
05:27 Marcus Lee: Also the ability to pin models and route by policy (region) helped keep data flows predictable.
05:34 Jordan Kim: Nice. For the podcast content, anything you want us to avoid saying publicly? Sensitive customers, exact contract amounts?
05:40 Lena Patel: Please avoid specific contract numbers, and don't name any of our end customers. High level metrics are fine.
05:46 Jordan Kim: Understood. We'll keep it high-level.
05:49 Jordan Kim: Quick technical aside — Maya, can you explain prefix/KV cache in 60 seconds for the listeners?
05:55 Maya Ortiz: Sure. So prefix caching stores repeated context (like prompts or docs) in a cached KV state so the runtime doesn't re-compute the early tokens every request. For Aurora, many of the prompts shared identical project metadata so cache hit rates were high and that reduced token compute and latency. There's also a tradeoff — cache consistency when prompt templates change, so we add cache invalidation rules in rollout pipelines.
06:19 Jordan Kim: Excellent. Back to marketing: we'll follow up with two artifacts — a short one-page case study draft and an edited audio clip. We'll need Lena's confirmation on the quotes.
06:30 Sofia Ruiz: That works. I'll coordinate review windows with PR and legal.
06:35 Jordan Kim: Any competitors or alternative strategies you considered before picking Redwood? Lena?
06:40 Lena Patel: We evaluated a couple of managed APIs like OpenAI and Anthropic for the hosted fast pilot, and we also considered building more orchestration ourselves on top of raw GPU instances. The managed APIs were easy but more variable cost; the raw build was too operationally heavy. Redwood hit the middle ground: low ops and cost controls.
06:58 Jordan Kim: Good summary. Rapid-fire — one thing you wish you knew before migrating? Marcus?
07:03 Marcus Lee: We'd have instrumented our prompt templates earlier and extracted common prefixes. That would have improved cache hit rates sooner.
07:11 Lena Patel: Also budget for a small burst of engineering time to tune tokenization edge cases — things like long output truncation behavior.
07:20 Jordan Kim: Both great tips. Listeners will appreciate those.
07:23 Jordan Kim: Let's open it up — any fun customer stories about how the feature helped a client?
07:28 Lena Patel: One customer used the auto-summary in a support triage flow and reduced time-to-resolution on certain tickets by 25% — they were able to auto-fill the triage notes which sped up handoffs.
07:40 Marcus Lee: Another customer used the deeper 13B analysis to generate weekly executive summaries and loved the consistency.
07:46 Jordan Kim: Nice. We're getting good material. Quick housekeeping — recording, editing, and approvals. Jordan to send outline and waiver; Lena to send quotes; Maya to share technical snippets. Any deadlines?
07:58 Sofia Ruiz: We'd like final quotes by 2025-10-27 and the waiver signed by 2025-10-24 to hit our November newsletter slot.
08:08 Jordan Kim: Got it. We'll align to those dates.
08:12 Jordan Kim: Any final thoughts?
08:15 Lena Patel: Thanks for making this easy. The team has enjoyed working with Redwood — it's been a relief to offload the infra.
08:24 Marcus Lee: Same.
08:26 Sofia Ruiz: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the final assets.
08:30 Jordan Kim: Great. We'll wrap and follow up with the three action items. Thanks all.
08:36 [end recording — informal chat continues off the record]
